summary: Improves TCP's resistance to blind in-window attacks by off-path attackers who try to inject spoofed packets. Larger windows and longer-lived connections, such as BGP, make guessing more feasible. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5961 changes how TCP checks some incoming packets. The checks make it harder for an attacker who cannot see the connection to disrupt it by guessing values.

subtitle: TCP checks resets, new connections, and acknowledgments more carefully.

tldr.problem: An off-path attacker who guesses a TCP connection can inject packets with sequence numbers inside its receive window, disrupting or corrupting the connection.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC tightens reset handling, challenges unexpected SYNs, and optionally restricts acceptable acknowledgment numbers for data segments.
tldr.outcome: The changes make blind injection harder but do not prevent it or protect against on-path attackers. RFC 9293 later updated this RFC.

facts.label: Mitigation strength
facts.value: RST SHOULD; SYN SHOULD; DATA MAY

today: RFC 5961 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2010. It has been updated by RFC 9293.

sections.title: How Blind In-Window Attacks Work
sections.content:
An off-path attacker forges the addresses and ports of an existing TCP connection, then guesses sequence numbers. A reset, SYN, or data segment accepted inside the receive window can disrupt the connection or affect its data.

The receive window makes guessing easier than searching the full sequence-number range. For a reset, the RFC estimates an average of 2^31 divided by the window size attempts, assuming the attacker knows the connection's four values.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker who cannot see a connection can still try forged packets. The larger the receive window, the more sequence numbers the receiver may accept.

sections.title: Checking Reset Segments
sections.content:
In a synchronized TCP state, an RST outside the receive window is silently dropped. An RST whose sequence number exactly matches RCV.NXT resets the connection.

An RST inside the window but not an exact match triggers a challenge ACK; TCP drops the RST and stops processing it. A legitimate peer that has already closed its connection responds to the challenge with a reset that can pass the exact-match test.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP no longer accepts every reset inside the receive window. It asks for confirmation unless the sequence number is exactly the next one expected.

sections.title: Checking SYN Segments
sections.content:
In a synchronized state, any SYN segment causes TCP to send a challenge ACK and discard the SYN, whatever its sequence number. A real peer that restarted can respond with a reset, after which the connection can be established again through SYN retransmission.

A forged SYN does not receive a useful response from the real peer and should not end the established connection. The RFC notes a rare corner case involving a restarted peer that reuses its address and port and selects a particular initial sequence number.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP challenges a SYN that arrives during an established connection. This gives a real peer a chance to confirm the restart before TCP closes the old connection.

sections.title: Narrowing the Acknowledgment Range
sections.content:
A blind attacker may try to inject data with a sequence number in the receive window. The optional data mitigation adds a stricter check for the acknowledgment number: it must fall between SND.UNA - MAX.SND.WND and SND.NXT.

Segments outside that range are discarded and an ACK is sent. The check reduces the chance of accepting false data and also makes forged FIN segments harder, but it does not eliminate false segments.
sections.plainLanguage: For the optional data defense, TCP checks both the sequence number and a narrower acknowledgment range. This reduces the chance that forged data will be accepted.

sections.title: Recommendations and ACK Throttling
sections.content:
The RST and SYN mitigations are SHOULD recommendations; the data-injection check is MAY. The RFC also recommends limiting challenge ACKs, since spoofed packets can trigger them. The example limit is 10 challenge ACKs in any 5-second window.

Administrators should be able to tune the count and time interval. A counter and timestamp can implement the limit without a timer.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP can limit how many challenge ACKs it sends in a period. This reduces unnecessary work when many packets trigger challenges.

sections.title: Protection and Remaining Risks
sections.content:
These rules make off-path injection harder, not impossible. They do not protect against an attacker who can observe the traffic; the RFC says IPsec AH or ESP is needed for full protection against on-path and off-path attacks.

Forged ICMP messages and middleboxes can also affect connections. Both endpoints need the mitigations for the connection to receive the full benefit, and ACK throttling can limit challenge traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The changes help against attackers who cannot see the connection. They do not stop someone who can observe its traffic.
